# Artificial intelligence literacy, readiness, and innovativeness: Exploring interrelationships in undergraduate nursing students

## S¸adiye Dur [a,](#nurse-education-today) Müge Cos¸gun˘ [b,\*,](#nurse-education-today) Ilknur Gol [c,](#nurse-education-today) Ozüm Erkin¨ [d,e](#nurse-education-today)

## ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT

### _Keywords:_ _Aim/objective:_ This study aimed to examine the relationships between AI literacy, medical AI readiness, and 

Artificial intelligence individual innovativeness among nursing students. Literacy _Background:_ Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare requires future nurses to develop competencies Readiness

in literacy, readiness, and innovativeness. Evidence on how these domains interrelate in nursing education re-

Innovativeness mains limited.

Nursing students Nursing education _Design:_ A cross-sectional, relational study design was adopted.

### _Methods:_ The study was conducted between April and July 2025 with 440 nursing students from two state 

universities in Türkiye. Data were collected online using a Descriptive Information Form, the AI Literacy Scale, the Medical AI Readiness Scale, and the Individual Innovativeness Scale. Descriptive statistics, independent samples _t_-test, one-way ANOVA, Mann–Whitney _U_ test, Kruskal–Wallis test, Pearson correlation, and multiple 

regression analysis were used.

### _Results:_ Students' mean age was 21.13 (SD = 2.80), and 70.5% were female. Most participants (91.4%) had not 

received prior AI training. University-based comparisons showed significant differences in AI literacy (_p_ = .042), medical AI readiness skills (_p_ = .006), and innovativeness (_p_ = .001). Demographic variables such as gender, grade level, AI training, usage frequency, and openness to new technologies were associated with scale scores. Correlation analyses revealed moderate positive associations between AI literacy and both medical AI readiness (_r_ = 0.532, _p \<_ .01) and innovativeness (_r_ = 0.423, p _\<_ .01). Regression analyses indicated that AI literacy (β = 0.475, _p \<_ .001) and individual innovativeness (β = 0.134, _p_ = .003) significantly predicted AI readiness, while 

university was not a significant predictor, and the model explained 29.8% of the variance.

### _Conclusions:_ AI literacy, readiness, and innovativeness are interrelated competencies among nursing students. 

Findings provide evidence for integrating AI-oriented content into curricula and for developing strategies that 

enhance students' preparedness for technology-driven healthcare.

Ronquillo et al., 2021). However, realizing this potential requires healthcare professionals and nursing students to possess adequate knowledge, skills, and readiness ([Akca Sumengen et al., 2025;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) Yalcin- kaya et al., 2024). AI literacy refers to individuals' ability to understand, evaluate, and effectively utilize AI applications ([Çelebi et al., 2023;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) [Chiu et al., 2024)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking). This competency is critical not only for adapting to tech- nological advancements but also for improving patient safety and care quality. AI readiness reflects the cognitive, skill-based, anticipatory, and ethical preparedness of individuals toward AI applications ([Karaca et al., 2021)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking). In this regard, it represents a key determinant of nursing students' capacity to embrace innovations and integrate them into care processes (Yalcinkaya et al., 2024).

AI literacy and medical AI readiness are conceptually related but represent distinct constructs within the broader framework of technol- ogy integration in healthcare. AI literacy primarily reflects individuals' knowledge, awareness, and critical understanding of artificial intelli- gence systems, including their capabilities, limitations, and ethical im- plications ([Chiu et al., 2024)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking). In contrast, medical AI readiness refers to the extent to which individuals feel cognitively, technically, and ethi- cally prepared to implement AI applications in clinical practice ([Karaca et al., 2021)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking). While AI literacy provides the foundational knowledge necessary to understand AI technologies, readiness reflects the practical preparedness required to apply these technologies in healthcare envi- ronments. Examining both constructs together therefore enables a more comprehensive understanding of how knowledge-based competencies translate into preparedness for AI-integrated clinical practice. Innovation is a concept that reflects individuals' openness to change, problem-solving abilities, and creative thinking skills (Roddy and Pol- fuss, 2020). In the field of healthcare, an innovative mindset enhances both professional development and the quality and efficiency of patient care ([Baksi et al., 2020)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking). The International Council of Nurses (ICN) de- fines innovation as “the process of developing new approaches, tech- nologies, and ways of working,” and emphasizes the pioneering role of nurses in implementing innovative care practices. The 2009 theme “Nursing and Innovation” highlighted the importance of innovation in delivering quality healthcare services ([International Council of Nurses (ICN), 2009)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking).

Today's healthcare systems require nurses who possess leadership skills, can think critically, and are capable of providing safe and high- quality care by effectively utilizing technology ([Heydari et al., 2023)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking). Therefore, strengthening nursing students' levels of AI literacy, AI readiness, and innovativeness during their education is considered critical for adapting to future AI-driven healthcare environments. Ac- cording to a recent systematic review by O'Connor et al. (2023), AI implementation in nursing education remains inconsistent, highlighting the need for empirical studies examining readiness and literacy collec- tively (O'Connor et al., 2023).

## 2. Background

The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare has begun to transform patient care, clinical decision support, di- agnostics, and health data management ([Bajwa et al., 2021;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) Sheikh et al., 2021). As this transformation unfolds, healthcare professionals are expected to develop competencies that enable them to adopt, evaluate, and effectively use AI-based systems. Nursing, as a discipline that plays a central role in health promotion, disease prevention, and direct patient care, occupies a key position in this technological shift (O'Connor et al., 2023). Accordingly, AI literacy—defined as the ability to understand, assess, and appropriately use AI applications—has emerged as a fundamental skill for nursing students and practitioners ([Çelebi et al., 2023;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) [Chiu et al., 2024)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking). Parallel to this, the concept of readiness for medical AI reflects the cognitive, technical, ethical, and anticipatory capacities required for nurses to engage with AI-driven practices in clinical environments ([Karaca et al., 2021)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking).

Alongside AI-related competencies, individual innovativeness is 

another essential attribute that supports the integration of technological advances into nursing education and practice. Innovation in healthcare is strongly associated with adaptability, problem-solving, and creative thinking, which are necessary to improve patient outcomes and increase the efficiency of clinical processes ([Baksi et al., 2020;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) Roddy and Polfuss, 2020). Recent literature suggests that innovation skills not only facili- tate the acceptance of emerging technologies but also enhance students' openness to adopting AI-based solutions ([Kaya et al., 2025;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) Ozdemir ¨ Aydın et al., 2025). Despite the growing emphasis on digital trans- formation in healthcare, there remains a scarcity of research simulta- neously examining AI literacy, readiness for medical AI, and individual innovativeness among nursing students. Addressing this gap is essential for guiding nursing curricula and policies that aim to prepare future professionals for AI-driven healthcare systems. The existing literature has not investigated these three domains together in the nursing student population.

Accordingly, the present study was designed to examine the levels of AI literacy, medical AI readiness, and individual innovativeness among nursing students, to explore their differences across demographic vari- ables, and to analyze the interrelationships among these constructs. Beyond these aims, a predictive model was also tested in which medical AI readiness was conceptualized as the outcome variable. This decision rests on the view that readiness reflects students' preparedness to inte- grate AI into nursing practice, whereas AI literacy (knowledge and skills) and innovativeness (a personal trait indicating openness to new ideas) are antecedent factors that are expected to influence readiness. Research questions 

- What are the levels of nursing students' artificial intelligence literacy, medical artificial intelligence readiness, and individual innovativeness?
- Do nursing students' levels of artificial intelligence literacy, medical artificial intelligence readiness, and individual innovativeness differ according to their demographic characteristics?
- Are there significant relationships among artificial intelligence lit- eracy, medical artificial intelligence readiness, and individual innovativeness?
- To what extent do artificial intelligence literacy and individual innovativeness predict nursing students' medical artificial intelli- gence readiness?

## 3. Methods

### _3.1._ _Design_

This study was conducted as a cross-sectional and correlational research. The research was reported in accordance with the Strength- ening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) statement ([Equator, 2023)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking).

### _3.2._ _Participants and setting_

The population of the study consisted of 1100 undergraduate nursing students enrolled in the nursing departments of two public universities in Türkiye between April and July 2025. The required sample size was initially estimated using the Yamane formula for known populations with a 95% confidence level, _p_ = .8, and a ± 5% margin of error, resulting in a minimum required sample of 285 participants. However, a total of 440 nursing students who met the inclusion criteria and voluntarily agreed to participate were included in the final sample. To further evaluate the adequacy of the sample size for the regression analysis, a post-hoc power analysis was conducted using G\*Power 3.1. Assuming two predictors, an alpha level of 0.05, and a medium effect size (f2 = 0.15), the achieved statistical power for the final sample size (_n_ = 440) was calculated as 0.99. This indicates that the study had sufficient statistical power to detect the relationships examined in the 

regression model. A non-probability convenience sampling strategy was used. Participation was voluntary, and the survey link was distributed through institutional communication channels including university email lists, student WhatsApp groups, and class representative networks. These channels were selected to reach nursing students across different year levels within the participating institutions. No financial or aca- demic incentives were offered to participants. Of the participants, 276 were from University A and 164 were from University B. In total, 440 students completed the questionnaire and met the eligibility criteria for inclusion in the analysis.

University A is located in Türkiye's third-largest city, which hosts five public and two foundation universities. Students at this university complete their clinical practices in multiple healthcare institutions, allowing them to gain broad experience with diverse patient pop- ulations. University B, on the other hand, is located in a smaller pro- vincial city with more limited clinical practice opportunities. The city has only one public hospital and no large-scale healthcare institutions with education and research status. Therefore, students' exposure to diverse cases and clinical experiences may be more restricted. The in- clusion criteria for the study were being over 18 years of age, having access to data collection forms via e-mail or social media tools, and volunteering to participate in the research.

### _3.3._ _Data collection tools_

#### _3.3.1._ _Student descriptive information form_

The descriptive information form was developed by the researchers based on the relevant literature ([Akca Sumengen et al., 2025;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) [Erol et al., 2018;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) Yalcinkaya et al., 2024). The form included basic information such as students' age, gender, marital status, university, year of study, whether they had received education on artificial intelligence, fre- quency of using AI applications, and openness to new technologies.

#### _3.3.2._ _Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale (AILS)_

The Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, originally developed by Wang et al. (2023), was adapted into Turkish and validated for reli- ability by [Çelebi et al. (2023)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) ([Çelebi et al., 2023;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) Wang et al., 2023). The scale consists of 12 items and four subdimensions—Evaluation, Ethics, Awareness, and Usage—parallel to the original form. It is scored on a 7-point Likert scale, with total scores ranging between 12 and 84. In the reliability analysis of the original study, Cronbach's alpha coefficient was 0.85. In the present study, the Cronbach's alpha internal consistency coefficient for the entire scale was calculated as 0.802.

#### _3.3.3._ _Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness (MAIR) Scale_

The Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale, developed by [Karaca et al. (2021),](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) is used to evaluate nursing students' readiness for medical AI ([Karaca et al., 2021)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking). The scale consists of 22 items across four subdimensions, rated on a 5-point Likert scale. Total scores range from 22 to 110, with higher scores indicating higher levels of readiness. The reliability analysis of the original study reported Cronbach's alpha coefficient of 0.877. In this study, Cronbach's alpha coefficient for the entire scale was calculated as 0.948.

#### _3.3.4._ _Individual Innovativeness Scale (IIS)_

The scale, originally developed by [Hurt et al. (1977),](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) was adapted into Turkish with validity and reliability established by Sarıoglu ˘ and Altuntas¸ ([Hurt et al., 1977;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) Sarıoglu ˘ Kemer and Altuntas¸, 2017). It consists of 18 items and three subdimensions. Scores range between 18 and 90, with classifications as follows: individuals scoring ≥80 are considered innovators, 69–80 early adopters, 57–68 interrogators, 46–56 skeptics, and _\<_46 traditionalists. In the original study, Cronbach's alpha reliability coefficient was 0.89, and in the present study it was calculated as 0.802.

### _3.4._ _Data collection_

Data collection commenced following the approval of the Ethics Committee for the conduct of this study. The data were collected be- tween April and July 2025 through an online survey administered via the Google Forms platform. Since the study aimed to reach a broader group rather than being limited to a single data collection site, data were obtained electronically by the researchers using a digital survey tool. The survey link was distributed to eligible nursing students through social media platforms. Prior to the main data collection, the question- naire was pilot-tested with a small group of nursing students to evaluate clarity and estimate completion time.

At the beginning of the four-section survey, an informed consent form was included on the first page, outlining the purpose, content, researchers, confidentiality of data, and voluntary nature of participa- tion. Only participants who read and consented to this form were allowed to proceed to the subsequent questions. Based on the pilot test results, the average completion time was approximately 15 min. Therefore, responses completed in less than 15 min were considered potentially inattentive and were excluded from the analysis. A total of 9 responses were excluded based on this criterion. Submission of the survey was considered confirmation of participants' consent to take part in the study. Common challenges associated with online surveys include item–response difficulties, low response rates, and representativeness issues (Polit and Beck, 2017). To mitigate these, several strategies were employed during the data collection process ([Berdida and Grande, 2023)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking). The survey was administered in the participants' native language, and verbal explanations were added for each Likert-scale item to ensure clarity. Additionally, the instruments were pilo_t_-tested prior to full administration to identify and resolve potential issues. To maintain data integrity, responses completed in less than 15 min were excluded from the final analysis. Given the participants' Turkish language proficiency, the instruments used had undergone Turkish validity and reliability testing.

### _3.5._ _Data analysis_

The data obtained from the study were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 25.0 software. Descriptive statistics included mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum values for continuous variables, and frequency (f) and percentage (%) values for categorical variables, presented in tabular form. Prior to analysis, normality tests were con- ducted to examine the distribution characteristics of the variables. For continuous variables, the Shapiro-Wilk test, skewness and kurtosis values, and Q-Q plots were utilized. Accordingly, appropriate para- metric and non-parametric tests (independent samples t-test, one-way ANOVA, Mann–Whitney U, and Kruskal–Wallis H) were used for group comparisons, and Pearson correlation analysis was performed to examine relationships between variables. Multiple linear regression analysis was conducted to examine the extent to which AI literacy and individual innovativeness predict AI readiness, with university included as a control variable. In addition, university was included as a control variable in the regression analysis. Bootstrap resampling (1000 samples, 95% CI) was performed to assess the robustness of the regression esti- mates. The internal consistency of the scales was assessed using Cron- bach's alpha reliability coefficient. A significance level of _p \<_ .05 was considered for all statistical analysis.

### _3.6._ _Ethical considerations_

Before the data collection process was initiated, ethics committee approval (IRB: 30.04.2025/2025/3-9) of the XX University Non- invasive Clinical Research Ethics Committee was obtained. Partici- pants were permitted to withdraw their responses both during and after the data collection period. The collected data was securely stored in a password-protected Google Drive, accessible only to the research team. 

Additionally, the study adhered to the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki, ensuring the protection of participants' identi- ties and the confidentiality of their data. Necessary permissions for the scales used in the research were obtained from the authors via e-mail.

The distribution of participants' Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale (AILS), Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness (MAIR), and Individual Innovativeness Scale (IIS) scores by demographic variables is presented in Table 3. Statistically significant differences were observed in MAIR scores by gender (U = 16,064.5, _p_ = .001). IIS scores differed signifi- cantly according to year of study (KW₍IIS₎ = 9.53, _p_ = .023). Students who had received AI training scored higher on IIS, and this difference was significant (U = 5953.0, _p_ = .024). Significant differences were also found in AILS (KW₍AILS₎ = 26.11, p = .000) and MAIR (KW₍MAIR₎ = 16.61, p = .001) scores based on the frequency of AI application use. Similarly, AILS (KW₍AILS₎ = 22.79, p = .000) and MAIR (KW₍MAIR₎ = 46.98, p = .000) scores differed significantly according to students' self- perceived level of AI knowledge. In addition, significant differences were observed in AILS (KW₍AILS₎ = 24.61, p = .000) and IIS (KW₍IIS₎ = 36.62, p = .000) scores depending on openness to new technologies. Pearson correlation analyses revealed moderate, positive, and sta- tistically significant relationships between AI literacy and medical AI readiness (_r_ = 0.532, _p \<_ .01) and between AI literacy and individual innovativeness (_r_ = 0.423, p _\<_ .01). In addition, a positive and statis- tically significant relationship of lower magnitude was found between medical AI readiness and individual innovativeness (_r_ = 0.335, p _\<_ .01). These findings suggest that individuals with higher levels of AI literacy tend to demonstrate greater readiness for medical AI applications as well as higher levels of individual innovativeness (Table 4).

nificant. **Model fit:** R[^2]= 0.298, Adjusted R[^2]= 0.293, F(3, 436) = 61.60, _p \<_ .001. with similar findings in both national and international literature. 

Several studies have reported that only a small proportion of nursing students have received AI education ([Abuzaid et al., 2022;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) [Hamedani et al., 2023;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) [Kwak et al., 2022;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) Ozdemir Aydın et al., 2025¨ ; Yalcinkaya et al., 2024). Similarly, [Akca Sumengen et al. (2025)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) and Yalcinkaya et al. (2024) emphasized that despite limited training experiences, stu- dents show strong curiosity about AI and a clear educational need ([Akca Sumengen et al., 2025;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) Yalcinkaya et al., 2024). This aligns with the current study's findings that students generally rated their knowledge as moderate while showing a high level of openness to new technologies. As highlighted in the literature ([De Gagne, 2023;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) Teng et al., 2022), the integration of AI into nursing curricula is regarded as a global necessity, and the quality and duration of educational content directly affect stu- dents' knowledge, attitudes, and readiness.

In comparisons between universities, students at University A scored higher in AI literacy and the skills dimension, which is noteworthy. This result parallels the findings of [Akca Sumengen et al. (2025)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) and Ozdemir ¨ Aydın et al. (2025), who highlighted that institutional differences and clinical practice experiences shape students' awareness of and ability to use AI. These findings suggest that the content of education, techno- logical resources, and teaching approaches in different institutions can influence students' knowledge and attitudes toward technology ([Chiu et al., 2024)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking). However, when university was included as a control var- iable in the regression analysis, it was not found to be a significant predictor of AI readiness. This suggests that individual-level factors, rather than institutional differences, play a more central role in explaining AI readiness among nursing students.

In particular, the finding that students scored higher in AI use and skills during periods of intensive clinical experience is consistent with previous studies ([Abou Hashish and Alnajjar, 2024;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) [Aydınlar et al., 2024)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking). The diversity of educational opportunities may be a determining factor in students' ability to adopt technology and develop innovative thinking.

The individual innovativeness scores of the participating students were found to be higher in the upper years of study. This supports studies emphasizing that as the educational process advances, students' problem-solving skills and innovative attitudes improve (Roddy and Polfuss, 2020). Furthermore, the finding that students who had received AI training demonstrated significantly higher levels of individual inno- vativeness suggests that education is an important factor in fostering innovative attitudes. Students who used AI applications more frequently, rated their knowledge as “good,” and reported openness to new technologies had higher scores in both AI Literacy Scale (AILS) and Medical AI Readiness (MAIR), underscoring the critical role of techno- logical experience and openness in the learning process ([Heydari et al., 2023)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking).

Correlation analyses revealed that AI Literacy was moderately and positively associated with both Medical AI Readiness and Individual Innovativeness. A low but significant positive relationship was also identified between Medical AI Readiness and Individual Innovativeness. These results indicate that individuals with higher AI literacy are more likely to display readiness for technology and maintain innovative at- titudes. Similar findings in the literature emphasize that individuals with higher levels of technology literacy tend to adopt innovative ways of thinking and adapt more easily to technological applications (O'Connor et al., 2023; Roddy and Polfuss, 2020). The strongest pre- dictor of AI readiness was identified as AI literacy (β = 0.475), while individual innovativeness also made a significant contribution (β = 0.134). The model explained 29.8% of the variance in AI readiness. This finding indicates that both cognitive and attitudinal readiness, along with innovative tendencies, are key determinants in the development of knowledge and skills related to AI. [Karaca et al. (2021)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) emphasized the critical role of cognitive and skill-based readiness in technology inte- gration among healthcare professionals, while the [ICN (2009)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) and O'Connor et al. (2023) highlighted the innovative leadership roles of nurses. Ozdemir Aydın et al. (2025)¨ and [Kaya et al. (2025)](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) demonstrated that innovative characteristics play a significant role in students' 

adaptation to AI and that individuals with higher innovativeness adapt more rapidly to technological advances. These results are consistent with the regression findings of the present study, suggesting that inno- vativeness is a factor that enhances nursing students' AI literacy. This study demonstrates that AI literacy, readiness, and innovative- ness are interconnected concepts among nursing students and should be addressed as a whole. The findings emphasize the importance of developing AI-focused curricula and creating innovative learning envi- ronments in nursing education, and they align with similar studies in the literature ([Akca Sumengen et al., 2025;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) [Kaya et al., 2025;](#students-and-professional-nurses-are-recommended-additionally-the-reported-in-this-paper-development-of-institutional-cultures-that-support-innovative-thinking) Ozdemir ¨ Aydın et al., 2025).

### _5.1._ _Strengths and limitations_

The most important contribution of this study is that it is among the first to examine artificial intelligence (AI) literacy, medical AI readiness, and individual innovativeness together in nursing students. In this respect, the study provides a new and valuable perspective to literature. Moreover, the fact that the sample size exceeded the calculated mini- mum requirement (_n_ = 440) allowed for stronger statistical evaluation of the findings. Another strength is that the scales used in this study had previously been validated for Turkish, and high internal consistency coefficients were also obtained here, supporting the reliability of the data.

However, several limitations should be taken into account. Since the study was limited to two universities, the generalization of the results to all nursing students should be made with caution. The use of self-report forms to collect data carries the risk of responses being influenced by social desirability bias. Given the cross-sectional design, the relation- ships among variables cannot be interpreted within a causal framework. Furthermore, as AI-related educational content and inter-institutional differences were not analyzed in detail, the sources of variation be- tween universities could not be fully explained.

### _5.2._ _Implications for nursing practice and policy_

The findings of this study present important implications for nursing education and health policies. First, the strong association of nursing students' artificial intelligence (AI) literacy with readiness and innova- tiveness highlights the necessity of including AI-related courses and practices in nursing curricula. AI-focused content should not be limited to theoretical knowledge but should also be reinforced with clinical scenarios and simulation-based applications.

The differences observed between the universities in this study particularly underscore the importance of clinical practice diversity. Students who have the opportunity to complete clinical experiences in multiple institutions encounter a broader variety of cases and healthcare delivery models, thereby enriching their learning processes. Conversely, when clinical practice opportunities are limited, students are exposed to fewer cases and experiences, which may indirectly influence both the competencies gained through education and their readiness for inno- vative technologies such as AI.

At the policy level, preparing nurses for AI technologies is crucial to ensuring the sustainability of digital transformation in healthcare sys- tems. National nursing education policies should include standards aimed at fostering students' technology literacy and innovative thinking skills. Moreover, in determining the locations where nursing schools are established, not only student enrollment capacity but also the adequacy of case diversity and clinical practice opportunities should be consid- ered. In this regard, the Ministry of Health and accreditation bodies for nursing education should take AI-focused core competencies and clinical practice diversity into account when updating curricula and planning educational institutions.

From a practice perspective, the adoption of AI technologies by nurses in clinical processes will enhance patient safety and the quality of care. Therefore, continuous education programs for both nursing 

### students and professional nurses are recommended. Additionally, the reported in this paper. development of institutional cultures that support innovative thinking
